q: Set out Madeira's ageing categories, and explain the change in the law regarding Tinta Negra.
accept: 3 5 10 15 20 30 40 50 plus colheita at five years frasqueira at twenty and tinta negra nameable since 2015
age indicated blends colheita and frasqueira with tinta negra now permitted on the label
five ten fifteen twenty year categories frasqueira twenty years in cask and tinta negra may now be named
ans: By ascending age: three-year Finest, five-year Reserve, ten-year Special Reserve, fifteen-year Extra Reserve, then twenty, thirty, forty and fifty year old wines, the figure in each case being an approved average age for a blend rather than a minimum for every component. Rainwater is a lighter, medium-dry blended style. Colheita, or Harvest, is a single vintage with a minimum of five years in cask. Frasqueira, also called Garrafeira, is the summit: a single vintage with a minimum of twenty years in cask, labelled with both the vintage and the bottling date. Style is set by grape — Sercial driest, then Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey, with Terrantez and Bastardo as the great rarities. Tinta Negra is the island's workhorse, the majority of the vineyard, and was for decades forbidden from appearing on a label, so it hid behind the sweetness descriptors instead. The rules changed in 2015: Tinta Negra may now be named as a varietal, and the result has been serious vintage-dated, colheita and aged Tinta Negra bottlings from Blandy's, Barbeito and Justino's.
exp: The Tinta Negra reform is commercial as much as legal: it converted the island's volume grape from anonymous filler into a category that can carry a vintage and a price. It is also the current-law answer where older texts still state flatly that the grape may not be named — quote the law and note that the books lag.

q: Name the five grapes generally regarded as Port's finest and say what each contributes to a blend.
accept: touriga nacional touriga franca tinta roriz tinta barroca and tinto cao
nacional franca roriz barroca and tinto cao with their blending roles
the five are touriga nacional touriga franca tinta roriz tinta barroca tinto cao
ans: Touriga Nacional gives perfume — violet, bergamot, black fruit — plus firm tannin and deep colour, but it is a shy, low-yielding, small-berried cropper. Touriga Franca is now the Douro's most planted variety: softer, floral, giving fruit sweetness, mid-palate flesh and elegance, and dependable in the vineyard. Tinta Roriz, which is Tempranillo, supplies body, colour and early ripening but shuts down badly in drought. Tinta Barroca ripens early and gives sugar, sweetness and softness, but bakes on hot south-facing terraces, so it is deliberately sited on cooler aspects and higher ground. Tinto Cão gives structure, acidity and ageing capacity from a tiny crop, which is why it nearly disappeared. Tinta Amarela, or Trincadeira, is frequently added as a sixth. The caveat matters as much as the list: most old Douro vineyards are field blends of dozens of co-planted varieties, many still poorly catalogued, so the five-grape orthodoxy is a modern replanting doctrine rather than a description of the historic terraces.
exp: The field-blend caveat is what separates a memorised list from an answer. A pre-phylloxera terrace at Vargellas or at Noval's Nacional contains varieties that have never been fully identified, and that co-planting — different ripening dates picked together — is part of why old-vine Douro wines taste as they do.

q: Take me through Vinho Verde beyond Alvarinho: its subregions, its other white grapes, and how the region has changed.
accept: nine subregions with loureiro avesso trajadura azal and pederna and a shift to serious still whites
moncao e melgaco lima cavado ave basto sousa amarante baiao and paiva with loureiro and avesso
the subregions plus loureiro trajadura avesso azal and the move away from spritz
ans: Nine subregions: Monção e Melgaço in the far north along the Minho, then Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva. Monção e Melgaço is the warmest and driest, sheltered from the Atlantic, and is Alvarinho country. Lima and Cávado are cooler and wetter and belong to Loureiro. Baião, in the east near the Douro, is Avesso — riper, fuller and lower in acid. Basto and Amarante grow more Azal and a good deal of red. The other whites are Loureiro, floral and laurel-scented and the region's most planted quality grape; Trajadura, which brings body and low acidity to blends; Avesso; Azal, sharp and late-ripening; and Arinto, known locally as Pedernã. Vinhão is the red, opaque and searingly acidic. The change is structural. The region has moved off pergolas and out of the old polyculture — vines trained up trees and along field margins above vegetables — onto properly trellised, dedicated vineyards; yields have fallen, the injected CO2 has been dropped from serious bottlings, alcohol has risen, and producers now make still, textured, lees- and oak-aged whites, single-subregion wines and even skin-contact and sparkling versions. Vinho Verde has become a place rather than a style.
exp: The name means green as in young, not green in colour, and the modern region is working to shed exactly the impression that word created. Being able to attach a grape to a subregion is how you demonstrate that you see the region as a mosaic rather than a single cheap category.

q: Describe the Dão — its geography, its grapes, and the political change that made modern Dão possible.
accept: a sheltered granite plateau with touriga nacional jaen alfrocheiro and encruzado plus the end of the cooperative monopoly
high granite basin ringed by the serra da estrela encruzado is the white and liberalisation followed eu accession
dao is granite at altitude home to touriga nacional and the coop monopoly ended after 1986
ans: A granite plateau in north-central Portugal at roughly 400 to 800 metres, ringed by mountains — the Serra da Estrela to the south and east, the Caramulo to the west, the Serra da Nave and Buçaco elsewhere — which shelter it from Atlantic rain and give cold winters, warm dry summers and markedly cool nights. Soils are sandy, weathered granite, with schist in places: infertile, free-draining and low in vigour, and the vineyard is broken into small parcels among pine and eucalyptus forest. Touriga Nacional is native here and Dão claims it; Jaen, which is Galicia's Mencía, gives soft, early-drinking red fruit; Alfrocheiro brings colour and structure; Tinta Roriz adds body; and Encruzado is the great white — textural, ageworthy, and handled with Burgundian technique, barrel fermentation and lees work. The political change is the spine of the story: for decades the law compelled growers to deliver their fruit to the regional co-operatives, which vinified badly at scale and gave Dão a national reputation for thin, dried-out, oxidised reds. Portugal's accession to the EEC in 1986 forced liberalisation and the monopoly ended at the close of that decade, allowing private estates — Quinta dos Roques, Quinta da Pellada and Quinta de Saes under Álvaro Castro, Casa da Passarella, Quinta da Ponte Pedrinha — to buy fruit and bottle their own wine. Essentially everything good about modern Dão dates from that moment.
exp: The co-operative story explains both halves of the region: why its old reputation was poor and why its best estates are so young. Set it against the Douro, where private shipping houses never surrendered control of quality, and the contrast makes the point far better than a list of grapes.

q: Portugal's fortified wines are not only Port and Madeira. Cover the others.
accept: moscatel de setubal carcavelos and moscatel do douro from favaios
setubal muscat carcavelos nearly extinct west of lisbon and favaios moscatel plus aged white port
moscatel de setubal moscatel do douro and the near extinct carcavelos
ans: Moscatel de Setúbal, on the Setúbal Peninsula south of Lisbon: a minimum of 85 per cent Muscat of Alexandria, fortified during fermentation and then aged with the skins steeping in the fortified wine for several months, which is what gives the orange-peel, raisin and marmalade intensity; five-year and twenty-year bottlings are the commercial norm, and Moscatel Roxo, from the pink-skinned mutation, is the rare collector's version. Carcavelos, a tiny DOC on the coast west of Lisbon, is a topaz-coloured, medium-sweet fortified from Galego Dourado, Ratinho and Arinto, all but obliterated by the suburban expansion of the Estoril coast and now reduced to token production kept alive largely by the Oeiras municipality's Villa Oeiras. Moscatel do Douro, centred on Favaios in the Cima Corgo, uses Moscatel Galego Branco — Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains — and gives a fresher, lighter, more floral Muscat than Setúbal's. And cask-aged white Port deserves its own mention, including ten- and twenty-year-old white Ports and the increasingly serious dry white apéritif style. The through-line beyond Port and Madeira is endangerment: Carcavelos is the textbook case of a DOC that urbanisation has nearly erased.
exp: Naming Carcavelos is an inexpensive way to show your map of Portugal has no blank spaces; explaining why it nearly died — the Estoril coast became a Lisbon suburb and the vineyard land became worth more built on — is what turns the name into an answer. Note too the parentage trap: Setúbal's Muscat is Alexandria, the Douro's is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.

corton since 2009 batard tiny
